nameStory: The "Six-celled Moss Dot" name comes from this tiny lichen's microscopic spores, which are divided into six compartments or cells. When you spot its small, dot-like fruiting bodies scattered across moss-covered surfaces, you're seeing the "dots" that inspired its common name.
description: Six-celled Moss Dot Lichen is a delicate crustose lichen that forms thin, almost invisible patches on moss and plant debris. This tiny species produces small, dark fruiting bodies (apothecia) that look like miniature black dots sprinkled across its substrate. Individual patches are usually less than an inch across, making this one of the more challenging lichens to notice without close inspection.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms extremely thin, nearly invisible crusts that blend seamlessly with moss surfaces and plant debris

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Tiny black dots (apothecia) about 0.5mm across with slightly raised rims - these are often the only visible sign of the lichen

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on moss, particularly on decaying moss cushions and organic debris in moist areas

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: The main body is pale gray to nearly colorless, often appearing whitish when dry and slightly darker when moist

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies rarely exceed 1-2 inches across, with the black fruiting bodies being the main identifying feature

habitat: Found in humid, shaded locations where moss thrives, particularly in coastal areas influenced by sea fog. Look for it in moist woodlands, on moss-covered rocks near streams, and in boggy areas where organic matter accumulates. Most common at lower elevations where moisture levels remain consistently high.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as spring moisture activates the moss substrate. The tiny black fruiting bodies are most prominent during this wet season.
seasonality.summer: May be harder to spot during dry spells when both the lichen and its moss host become less conspicuous. Early morning dew can help reveal colonies.
seasonality.fall: Autumn rains bring out the best visibility as moss cushions plump up and the contrast between the dark fruiting bodies and pale thallus becomes clearer.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but may be obscured by snow. On mild winter days with good moisture, it can be easier to spot than in dry summer conditions.

funFact: This lichen is so tiny and inconspicuous that it was likely overlooked by naturalists for decades - the single observation record in New England suggests it might be either extremely rare or simply hiding in plain sight on countless moss patches that no one has examined closely enough!
confusionNotes: The tiny black dots could be mistaken for moss reproductive structures (sporangia) or even specks of dirt. The key difference is that lichen apothecia have a slightly raised, rim-like edge and remain consistently round, while moss sporangia are usually on stalks and dirt particles are irregular in shape.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "moss dot" lichen, this species doesn't harm the moss it grows on - it's simply using the moss as a stable, moist platform. The relationship is more like a tiny tenant living on a green apartment building than a parasite.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Bilimbia fuscoviridis, Six-celled Moss Dot Lichen is more specialized for moss substrates and has smaller fruiting bodies. While both produce dark apothecia, fuscoviridis tends to grow on soil and rock rather than exclusively on moss, and typically forms slightly more visible crusts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bilimbia fuscoviridis differs from its relative Six-celled Moss Dot Lichen by preferring bark over soil or rock substrates and showing more pronounced green coloration when wet.
